summary: Describes how GSS-API domain-based service principal names are mapped onto Kerberos V principal names. It is the Kerberos mechanism companion to the general domain-based names specification. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Kerberos has its own style of names. This paper translates one kind of service name into the matching Kerberos name, like converting a nickname into a formal name.

questions: how do gss-api domain-based names map to kerberos
what is a kerberos principal name
subtitle: How a domain-based GSS-API service name becomes a three-part Kerberos V principal name.

tldr.problem: GSS-API domain-based service names carry a service, a hostname and a domain, and the Kerberos V mechanism needs a rule for turning them into Kerberos principal names.
tldr.mechanism: The service, hostname and domain become the first, second and third components of the principal name, and the realm is the one that corresponds to the domain name.
tldr.outcome: For example, ldap@foo.example@ds1.foo.example may map to ldap/ds1.foo.example/foo.example@FOO.EXAMPLE. The realm must be derived from the domain slot, not the hostname slot.

today: RFC 5179 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this RFC.

sections.title: Mapping Domain-Based Names
sections.content:
Following RFC 5178, this document gives the Kerberos V specifics for GSS-API domain-based service names (name type GSS_C_NT_DOMAINBASED_SERVICE). Such names SHOULD be mapped to Kerberos V principal names as follows:

  • the service becomes the first (0th) component;
  • the hostname becomes the second component;
  • the domain name becomes the third component;
  • the realm is the one that corresponds to the domain name, treated as a hostname.

The same name canonicalization considerations apply as elsewhere in the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism and in Kerberos V generally.
sections.eli5: The three pieces of the nickname are lined up in order: service first, then host, then domain.

sections.title: Name Type
sections.content: Implementations SHOULD use the Kerberos V name type NTT-SRVT-HST-DOMAIN, which has the value 12. They MAY use NT-UNKNOWN instead.
sections.eli5: The name gets a label saying what kind of name it is. There is a preferred label and a fallback.

sections.title: Examples and Internationalization
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples. The domain-based name ldap@foo.example@ds1.foo.example may map to ldap/ds1.foo.example/foo.example@FOO.EXAMPLE, and kadmin@foo.example@kdc1.foo.example may map to kadmin/kdc1.foo.example/foo.example@FOO.EXAMPLE.

The RFC says it is unclear how best to handle internationalization because the Kerberos V core internationalization work was incomplete. It requires implementations to use ACE-encoded internationalized domain names for the hostname and domain slots.
sections.eli5: Names with accents or other alphabets are written in a plain-letter code so everyone can read them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC refers to RFC 5178 for security considerations. It adds that, for security, the realm of a domain-based principal name must be derived from the hostname slot rather than the domain name slot of the input string.
sections.eli5: Pick the right piece of the name to decide which realm to trust, or you could end up trusting the wrong one.
